title: "Growing Java's rice in a computer, one weather cell at a time"

```{ojs}
import {withDownload, adminMarks, cellFeatures, fmt, pearson} from "../assets/js/dl.js"
summary = FileAttachment("data/summary.json").json()
cells = FileAttachment("data/grid_cells.csv").csv({typed: true})
districtsGeo = FileAttachment("data/districts.geojson").json()
outline = FileAttachment("data/java_outline.geojson").json()
provinces = FileAttachment("data/provinces.geojson").json()
districts = FileAttachment("data/districts.csv").csv({typed: true})
javaYears = FileAttachment("data/java_years.csv").csv({typed: true})
cur = summary.current
calRun = summary.current_run
uncalRun = Object.entries(summary.districts).find(([k, v]) => v.slpf == null && v.tcldf == null)?.[0] ?? calRun
runOptions = new Map(Object.entries(summary.districts).map(([k, v]) => [v.label, k]))
cal = summary.districts[calRun]
uncal = summary.districts[uncalRun]
runs = FileAttachment("data/runs.json").json()
// earlier calibration: one SLPF for all rice, no TCLDF change
oneRun = Object.entries(summary.districts).find(([k, v]) => v.slpf != null && v.tcldf == null && v.slpf_rainfed == null)?.[0] ?? calRun
one = summary.districts[oneRun]
oneInfo = runs.find(r => r.run === oneRun)
fit = FileAttachment("data/fit_slpf.json").json()
```

```{ojs}
kpis = html`<div class="kpi-row">
  <div class="kpi"><div class="v">${fmt.int(cur.seasons)}</div><div class="l">rice seasons simulated for Java (season years ${JSON.parse(cur.years).join("-")})</div></div>
  <div class="kpi"><div class="v">${fmt.int(cur.failed)}</div><div class="l">seasons the engine rejected</div></div>
  <div class="kpi"><div class="v">${fmt.d1(cur.minutes)} min</div><div class="l">wall time, ${cur.workers} engine processes in parallel</div></div>
  <div class="kpi"><div class="v">${fmt.int(cur.cells)}</div><div class="l">0.1° weather cells with rice (${fmt.int(cur.strata)} strata)</div></div>
  <div class="kpi"><div class="v">${fmt.d2(cur.ha / 1e6)} M ha</div><div class="l">rice fields covered, from 100 m maps</div></div>
</div>`
```

::: {.source-note}
Every number on this page is read from `docs/java/data/` when the page loads; those files are exported from the
current run, ${calRun}, exported ${summary.generated} by `docs/scripts/export_data.py`. When the
calibration changes, the numbers change with it. See [Rebuild](../rebuild.qmd).

## A crop model built for one field

DSSAT, the Decision Support System for Agrotechnology Transfer, is one of the most used families of crop
models in the world [@jones2003]. Its rice model, CERES-Rice, grows a crop day by day from the weather: how
much sunlight the leaves catch, how warm the nights are, how much water and nitrogen the roots find. Feed it
the weather, the soil and the farmer's calendar for one field, and it tells you when the crop flowers, when it
matures, and how much grain it yields.

That "one field" is both its strength and its limit. DSSAT was designed around field experiments: one plot,
one weather station, one soil profile, a handful of treatments. Indonesia's rice is not one field. It is a
mosaic of about 7.4 million hectares of paddies (7,392,188 ha in the national 100 m raster built from the
ATR/BPN 2024 rice-field map, `temp/inputs-detail.md`), from irrigated lowlands on the north coast of Java to
rain-fed terraces in the hills, with planting dates that follow the monsoon.

## What xdssat does

**xdssat runs the unmodified DSSAT engine over a grid.** It does not rewrite the model. For every 0.1 degree
weather cell that holds rice, and for every season, it writes the ordinary DSSAT input files (a weather file, a
soil profile and an experiment file), runs the stock `dscsm048` executable on hundreds of those cell-seasons at
a time, in parallel, and gathers the results into one gridded netCDF file that GIS tools and climate tools can
read.

```{mermaid}
%%{init: {"theme": "neutral"}}%%
flowchart TB
  A[AgERA5 daily weather<br/>0.1 degree netCDF] --> D
  B[SoilGrids 2.0<br/>250 m GeoTIFF] --> D
  C[Rice fields, irrigation,<br/>districts: 100 m rasters] --> D
  D[Strata:<br/>weather cell x water regime] --> E[WTH + SOL + FileX<br/>per chunk]
  E --> F[dscsm048 x 32<br/>in parallel]
  F --> G[summary.csv]
  G --> H[CF netCDF<br/>system x year x lat x lon]
  H --> I[Compare with<br/>district statistics]
```

For Java that means ${fmt.int(cur.cells)} weather cells, ${fmt.int(cur.strata)} strata (a cell's
irrigated rice and its rain-fed rice are simulated separately) and ${fmt.int(cur.seasons)} seasons over 30
agricultural years, in ${fmt.d1(cur.minutes)} minutes.

The map shows the simulated mean yield of each cell. Pick a season and water regime.

```{ojs}
viewof sysPick = Inputs.radio(
  new Map([["Wet season, irrigated", "wet_irrigated"], ["Wet season, rain-fed", "wet_rainfed"], ["Dry season, irrigated", "dry_irrigated"]]),
  {value: "wet_irrigated", label: "System"})
```

```{ojs}
yieldMap = {
  const col = `hwah_${sysPick}`;
  const rows = cells.filter(d => d[col] != null && isFinite(d[col]));
  const fc = cellFeatures(rows);
  const w = Math.min(width, 960);
  return withDownload(Plot.plot({
    width: w, height: Math.round(w * 0.42),
    projection: {type: "mercator", domain: outline},
    color: {type: "linear", scheme: "YlGn", legend: true, label: "Mean simulated yield, kg/ha dry matter", domain: [2500, 7000], clamp: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.geo(provinces, {fill: "#f1f1f1", clip: true}),
      Plot.geo(fc.features, Plot.centroid({fill: d => d.properties[col], stroke: null,
        title: d => `cell ${d.properties.lat.toFixed(1)}, ${d.properties.lon.toFixed(1)}\n${fmt.int(d.properties[col])} kg/ha\nseason ${fmt.d1(d.properties["len_" + sysPick])} d`, tip: true})),
      ...adminMarks(Plot, provinces, districtsGeo)
    ]
  }), `xdssat-java-mean-yield-${sysPick}`, "Hover a cell for its value.");
}
```

::: {.source-note}
Mean of the seasonal DSSAT yield (`HWAH`) over 1991-2020 season years, per cell and system, from
`summary.csv` of the current run. Colour scale clamped at 2,500 and 7,000 kg/ha. District outlines: BPS admin2
boundaries.
:::

## Why simulate rice on a grid at all?

Because the questions people ask about rice in Indonesia are spatial. Where would a dry year hurt most? Which
districts are already close to what their weather allows, and which have room to grow? How would a shift in the
monsoon onset move the planting calendar, district by district? A single-field model answers none of these. A
model run on every cell, with each cell's own weather, soil and calendar, can, as long as its results can be
checked against what farmers actually harvest.

That check is the point of the Java pilot. Indonesia publishes harvested area, production and yield for every
district (*kabupaten* and *kota*) every year. xdssat adds the simulated seasons up the same way: by the
calendar year of harvest, weighted by the rice area of each cell in each district, and converted from the
model's dry matter to the dry milled-grain basis (*gabah kering giling*, GKG) of the statistics. Details are on
the [Scientific method](science.qmd) page.

## What the Java results show so far

### The level: calibrated

Out of the box, with full irrigation for irrigated fields and 140 kg of nitrogen per hectare, the model grew
far more rice than Java harvests: ${fmt.d2(uncal.level_area_weighted)} times the district statistics on
average (run ${uncalRun}). That is expected. A crop model simulates the yield that weather, water and
nitrogen allow; real fields also lose yield to pests, diseases, weeds, uneven water and management that the
model does not know about.

xdssat closes that gap with the soil fertility factor `SLPF` of DSSAT, which scales the crop's daily
carbohydrate production, fitted to the district statistics (`scripts/fit_slpf.py`). In the current run SLPF
differs by water regime and with the cell's season night temperature: ${slpfText}. The run also raises the
cold-sterility threshold TCLDF to ${cur.tcldf} °C (both explained on the
[Scientific method](science.qmd#slpf) page). Simulated and observed Java means agree: ${fmt.d1(cal.java_sim)} simulated vs ${fmt.d1(cal.java_obs)} observed quintal per hectare (GKG), and the province ratios range
from ${fmt.d2(d3.min(Object.values(cal.province_ratio)))} to ${fmt.d2(d3.max(Object.values(cal.province_ratio)))}.

```{ojs}
viewof runPick = Inputs.select(runOptions, {value: calRun, label: "Run", width: 460})
```

```{ojs}
javaChart = {
  const rows = javaYears.filter(d => d.run === runPick).flatMap(d => [
    {year: d.year, series: "Simulated", value: d.sim},
    {year: d.year, series: "Observed (BDSP/BPS)", value: d.obs}]);
  return withDownload(Plot.plot({
    width: Math.min(width, 900), height: 340, marginLeft: 50,
    y: {label: "Java rice yield, ku/ha GKG", grid: true, zero: false},
    x: {label: "Harvest year", tickFormat: d => String(d)},
    color: {legend: true, domain: ["Simulated", "Observed (BDSP/BPS)"], range: ["#2a7f62", "#d9822b"]},
    marks: [
      Plot.lineY(rows, {x: "year", y: "value", stroke: "series", strokeWidth: 2, tip: true}),
      Plot.dot(rows, {x: "year", y: "value", fill: "series", r: 3, tip: true})
    ]
  }), `xdssat-java-yield-${runPick}`);
}
```

::: {.source-note}
Java mean per harvest year, weighted by the rice area of each district, over the districts with an observed
yield that year (the same weighting `scripts/compare_districts.py` prints). Observed: district yields from the
Ministry of Agriculture BDSP portal [@bdsp], cleaned by `scripts/clean_bdsp.py`. Simulated: dry matter / 0.86
(14% grain moisture, an assumption; see [Scientific method](science.qmd#gkg)).
:::

### The map: better, not yet right

Getting the Java average right is the easy part; one factor can do it. Getting the *pattern* right is harder.
The map shows simulated over observed yield for each district; switch runs to see how the calibration steps
changed it.

```{ojs}
viewof ratioRun = Inputs.select(runOptions, {value: calRun, label: "Run", width: 460})
```

```{ojs}
ratioMap = {
  const by = new Map(districts.filter(d => d.run === ratioRun).map(d => [String(d.code), d]));
  const w = Math.min(width, 960);
  const center = 1;
  const half = Math.max(0.45, d3.max(districts.filter(d => d.run === ratioRun), d => Math.abs(d.ratio - 1)));
  return withDownload(Plot.plot({
    width: w, height: Math.round(w * 0.42),
    projection: {type: "mercator", domain: outline},
    color: {type: "diverging", scheme: "PuOr", pivot: center, reverse: true, legend: true,
            label: "Simulated / observed yield, district mean", domain: [center - half, center + half], clamp: true},
    marks: [
      Plot.geo(districtsGeo.features.filter(f => f.properties.java), {fill: "#e4e4e4", stroke: "none"}),
      Plot.geo(districtsGeo.features.filter(f => by.has(f.properties.code)), {
        fill: f => by.get(f.properties.code).ratio, stroke: "#666", strokeWidth: 0.4,
        title: f => { const d = by.get(f.properties.code); return `${d.name} (${d.province})\nobs ${fmt.d1(d.obs_mean)} / sim ${fmt.d1(d.sim_mean)} ku/ha\nratio ${fmt.d2(d.ratio)}, ${d.years} years`; }}),
      ...adminMarks(Plot, provinces, districtsGeo)
    ]
  }), `xdssat-district-ratio-${ratioRun}`, "Grey: fewer than 1,000 ha of simulated rice or fewer than 5 observed years.");
}
```

The current run sits within ${fmt.d2(cal.ratio_p10)} to ${fmt.d2(cal.ratio_p90)} of the observed yield in 80%
of the districts (10th to 90th percentile). Across the ${cal.districts} districts compared, the correlation
between observed and simulated district means is r = ${fmt.d2(cal.spatial_r)}, and the standard deviation of
the district means is ${fmt.d1(cal.sim_sd_districts)} ku/ha simulated against ${fmt.d1(cal.obs_sd_districts)} observed.

With one SLPF for all rice and the default TCLDF (run ${oneRun}), that correlation was r = ${fmt.d2(one.spatial_r)}, with a spread of ${fmt.d1(one.sim_sd_districts)} ku/ha: the districts the model ranked high
were not the ones that harvest most. That run is preselected in the chart below; the colour shows why.

```{ojs}
viewof scatterRun = Inputs.select(runOptions, {value: oneRun, label: "Run", width: 460})
```

```{ojs}
scatter = {
  const rows = districts.filter(d => d.run === scatterRun);
  const hasLen = rows.some(d => d.season_len != null && isFinite(d.season_len));
  return withDownload(Plot.plot({
    width: Math.min(width, 640), height: 420, marginLeft: 50,
    x: {label: "Observed district mean, ku/ha GKG", grid: true},
    y: {label: "Simulated district mean, ku/ha GKG", grid: true},
    color: hasLen ? {type: "linear", scheme: "Viridis", legend: true, label: "Simulated season length, days"} : undefined,
    marks: [
      Plot.line([[40, 40], [d3.max(rows, d => Math.max(d.sim_mean, d.obs_mean)), d3.max(rows, d => Math.max(d.sim_mean, d.obs_mean))]], {stroke: "#aaa", strokeDasharray: "4,3"}),
      Plot.dot(rows, {x: "obs_mean", y: "sim_mean", fill: hasLen ? "season_len" : "#2a7f62", r: 4, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 0.5,
        tip: true, channels: {District: "name", Province: "province", "Season, d": "season_len"}})
    ]
  }), `xdssat-district-obs-vs-sim-${scatterRun}`);
}
```

In that run, simulated district yield followed the simulated season length (r = ${fmt.d2(rLenSim)}), and
season length followed night temperature (r = ${fmt.d2(rLenTmin)} with the mean daily minimum). The longest
simulated seasons were in ${longest}. In CERES-Rice development runs on thermal time, so a cooler crop
takes more days to mature and has more days to build biomass. Observed yields show no such bonus
(r = ${fmt.d2(rLenObs)} with simulated season length); they are, if anything, higher where more of the rice is
irrigated (r = ${fmt.d2(rIrrObs)}; simulated: r = ${fmt.d2(rIrrSim)}), while the model gave rain-fed strata
more than irrigated ones in the wet season: ${fmt.int(oneInfo?.yield_wet_rainfed)} vs ${fmt.int(oneInfo?.yield_wet_irrigated)} kg/ha.

Three steps address these. Raising TCLDF to ${cur.tcldf} °C makes cool nights during panicle development
cost grains, which reduces the highland bonus but does not remove it. A separate SLPF for rain-fed rice lowers
rain-fed yields. Finally, letting SLPF fall with the cell's mean season minimum temperature takes out most of
the remaining bonus of the cool, long-season cells: wet-season yield in the current run is ${fmt.int(cur.yield_wet_irrigated)} kg/ha for irrigated and ${fmt.int(cur.yield_wet_rainfed)} kg/ha for rain-fed
strata. Each step was checked with full runs against the districts:

```{ojs}
calSteps = [
  {step: "1. One SLPF", run: oneTcRun, fitKey: "one"},
  {step: "2. Irrigated / rain-fed pair", run: pairRun, fitKey: "two"},
  {step: "3. Pair + Tmin slope (current)", run: calRun, fitKey: "temp"}
].filter(d => d.run && summary.districts[d.run]).map(d => {
  const v = summary.districts[d.run];
  const ho = d3.sum(fit.cv, c => c.districts * c[`${d.fitKey}_rmse_log`]) / d3.sum(fit.cv, c => c.districts);
  return {Calibration: d.step, Run: d.run, "RMSE log": v.rmse_log, "Within ±10%": v.within10, "Spatial r": v.spatial_r,
          "SD sim / obs, ku/ha": `${fmt.d1(v.sim_sd_districts)} / ${fmt.d1(v.obs_sd_districts)}`, "Held-out RMSE log": ho};
})
Inputs.table(calSteps, {format: {"RMSE log": d => d.toFixed(3), "Within ±10%": fmt.pct, "Spatial r": fmt.d2, "Held-out RMSE log": d => d.toFixed(3)}, layout: "auto"})
```

::: {.source-note}
All three with TCLDF ${cur.tcldf}. RMSE log: rice-area weighted root mean square of log(simulated/observed)
over the ${cal.districts} district means. Within ±10%: share of districts whose ratio is between 0.9 and 1.1.
Held-out: each province's districts scored with parameters fitted without that province
(`fit_slpf.py` leave-one-province-out), averaged over districts.
:::

```{ojs}
oneRows = districts.filter(d => d.run === oneRun)
rLenSim = pearson(oneRows.map(d => d.season_len), oneRows.map(d => d.sim_mean))
rLenObs = pearson(oneRows.map(d => d.season_len), oneRows.map(d => d.obs_mean))
rLenTmin = pearson(oneRows.map(d => d.season_len), oneRows.map(d => d.tmina))
rIrrObs = pearson(oneRows.map(d => d.irr_share), oneRows.map(d => d.obs_mean))
rIrrSim = pearson(oneRows.map(d => d.irr_share), oneRows.map(d => d.sim_mean))
longest = oneRows.filter(d => d.season_len != null).sort((a, b) => b.season_len - a.season_len).slice(0, 4).map(d => `${d.name} (${Math.round(d.season_len)} d, Tmin ${fmt.d1(d.tmina)} °C)`).join(", ")
fitPair = `${fit.two.slpf_irrigated} irrigated / ${fit.two.slpf_rainfed} rain-fed`
pairRun = Object.entries(summary.districts).find(([k, v]) => v.slpf_rainfed != null && v.tcldf != null)?.[0]
oneTcRun = Object.entries(summary.districts).find(([k, v]) => v.slpf != null && v.slpf < 1 && v.slpf_rainfed == null && !v.slpf_table && v.tcldf != null)?.[0]
slpfText = fit.temp
  ? `${fmt.d2(fit.temp.slpf_irrigated)} for irrigated and ${fmt.d2(fit.temp.slpf_rainfed)} for rain-fed strata at a mean season minimum of ${fit.temp.tref} °C, changing by ${fit.temp.slope_per_C.toFixed(4)} per °C of the cell's minimum and kept within ${d3.min(fit.slpf_points)}-${d3.max(fit.slpf_points)}`
  : `${cur.slpf} for irrigated and ${cur.slpf_rainfed} for rain-fed strata`
calRows = districts.filter(d => d.run === calRun)
rLenSimCal = pearson(calRows.map(d => d.season_len), calRows.map(d => d.sim_mean))
```

## The honest gaps

::: {.gap-box}
**The spatial pattern is partly fitted, not simulated.** Both the rain-fed SLPF and its temperature slope are
statistical corrections. They lower rain-fed yields and the yields of cool, long-season cells because the
district data say so, not because the model simulates what limits them (water, nutrients, management, the
varieties actually grown in the highlands). The leave-one-province-out test in `fit_slpf.py` checks that
they also predict districts they were not fitted on ([Scientific method](science.qmd#slpf-temp)), but the
mechanism is open. Spatial r is ${fmt.d2(cal.spatial_r)}: the district levels fit (RMSE log ${cal.rmse_log.toFixed(3)}), but which
districts harvest more than others is still only partly reproduced. The correlation of simulated district yield with season length is down to r = ${fmt.d2(rLenSimCal)}, from ${fmt.d2(rLenSim)} with one SLPF, largely because the SLPF slope was fitted against it.
:::

::: {.gap-box}
**Year-to-year swings do not match.** After removing the trend, the median correlation between simulated and
observed yield of a district over the years is ${fmt.d2(cal.r_detrended_median)}
with ${fmt.pct(cal.r_detrended_pos)} of districts above zero; against a 5-year running mean instead of a
linear trend, the median is ${fmt.d2(cal.r_highpass_median)} with ${fmt.pct(cal.r_highpass_pos)} above zero. The model's year-to-year swings follow solar
radiation; the observed ones come partly in multi-year blocks that look non-weather (programmes, statistical
methods), and a water-shortage explanation was tested and not supported (`HANDOFF.md`, findings of
2026-11-06).
:::

::: {.gap-box}
**No trend.** Observed Java yield rises by ${fmt.sign1(cal.java_obs_trend_decade)} ku/ha per decade, the model
by ${fmt.sign1(cal.java_sim_trend_decade)}: the cultivar (IR 58) and nitrogen rate are held fixed for 30
years, so technology change is outside the model.
:::

::: {.gap-box}
**Assumptions still standing.** Planting dates come from a rainfall-onset rule with placeholder offsets
(transplanting 20 days after onset, dry season 120 days after the wet season); the GKG moisture of 14% is
assumed, not taken from a BPS definition; the older uniform and by-zone calendar runs predate a bug fix and are
stale; ${calendarReruns}.

```{ojs}
calendarReruns = {
  const r = runs.filter(d => (d.mode === "uniform" || d.mode === "by_zone") && d.slpf_table && d.slpf_table !== "None");
  return r.length ? `reruns with the current calibration: ${r.map(d => d.run).join(", ")}` : "they have not been rerun with the current calibration";
}
```
:::
